{{Short description|Partial differential equations describing diffusion}}
The '''Kolmogorov backward equation (KBE)''' and its [[Adjoint of an operator|adjoint]], the Kolmogorov forward equation, are [[partial differential equation]]s (PDE) that arise in the theory of continuous-time continuous-state [[Markov process]]es.  Both were published by [[Andrey Kolmogorov]] in 1931.<ref name="k31">Andrei Kolmogorov, "Über die analytischen Methoden in der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung" (On Analytical Methods in the Theory of Probability), 1931, [http://eudml.org/doc/159476]</ref>  Later it was realized that the forward equation was already known to physicists under the name [[Fokker&ndash;Planck equation]];  the KBE on the other hand was new.

==Overview==
The Kolmogorov forward equation is used to evolve the state of a system forward in time. Given an initial [[probability distribution]] <math>p_t(x)</math> for a system being in state <math>x</math> at time <math>t,</math> the forward PDE is integrated to obtain <math>p_s(x)</math> at later times <math>s>t.</math> A common case takes the initial value <math>p_t(x)</math> to be a [[Dirac delta function]] centered on the known initial state <math>x.</math>

The Kolmogorov backward equation is used to estimate the probability of the current system evolving so that its future state at time <math>s>t</math> is given by some fixed probability function <math>p_s(x).</math> That is, the probability distribution in the future is given as a boundary condition, and the backwards PDE is integrated backwards in time.

A common boundary condition is to ask that the future state is contained in some subset of states <math>B,</math> the '''target set'''. Writing the [[membership function|set membership function]] as <math>1_B,</math> so that <math>1_B(x)=1</math> if <math>x\in B</math> and zero otherwise, the backward equation expresses the '''hit probability''' <math>p_t(x)</math> that in the future, the set membership will be sharp, given by <math>p_s(x) = 1_B(x)/\Vert B\Vert.</math> Here, <math>\Vert B\Vert</math> is just the size of the set <math>B,</math> a normalization so that the total probability at time <math>s</math> integrates to one.

== Kolmogorov backward equation ==

Let <math>\{X_{t}\}_{0 \le t \le T}</math> be the solution of the [[stochastic differential equation]]

:<math>
dX_t \;=\; \mu\bigl(t, X_t\bigr)\,dt \;+\; \sigma\bigl(t, X_t\bigr)\,dW_t,
\quad 0 \;\le\; t \;\le\; T,
</math>

where <math>W_t</math> is a (possibly multi-dimensional) [[Wiener process]] ([[Brownian motion]]), <math>\mu</math> is the drift coefficient, and <math>\sigma</math> is related to the [[diffusion coefficient]] <math>D</math> as <math>D=\sigma^2/2.</math> Define the [[transition density]] (or [[fundamental solution]]) <math>p(t,x;\,T,y)</math> by

:<math>
p(t,x;\,T,y)
\;=\;
\frac{\mathbb{P}[\,X_T \in dy \,\mid\, X_t = x\,]}{dy},
\quad
t < T.
</math>

Then the usual Kolmogorov backward equation for <math>p</math> is

:<math>
\frac{\partial p}{\partial t}(t, x;\,T, y)
\;+\;
A\, p(t, x;\,T, y)
\;=\;
0,
\quad
\lim_{t \to T}\, p(t,x;\,T,y)
\;=\;
\delta_{y}(x),
</math>

where <math>\delta_{y}(x)</math> is the [[Dirac delta]] in <math>x</math> centered at <math>y</math>, and <math>A</math> is the [[infinitesimal generator (stochastic processes)|infinitesimal generator]] of the diffusion:

:<math>
A\,f(x)
\;=\;
\sum_{i}\,\mu_{i}(x)\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}(x)
\;+\;
\frac12\,\sum_{i,j}\,
  \bigl[\sigma(x)\,\sigma(x)^{\mathsf{T}}\bigr]_{ij}\,
  \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_{i}\,\partial x_{j}}(x).
</math>

== Feynman–Kac formula ==
The backward Kolmogorov equation can be used to derive the [[Feynman–Kac formula]]. Given a function <math>F</math> that satisfies the boundary value problem

:<math>
\frac{\partial F}{\partial t}(t,x)
\;+\;
\mu(t,x)\,\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}(t,x)
\;+\;
\frac{1}{2}\,\sigma^2(t,x)\,\frac{\partial^2 F}{\partial x^2}(t,x)
\;=\;
0,
\quad
0 \le t \le T,
\quad
F(T,x) \;=\; \Phi(x)
</math>

and given <math>\{X_t\}_{0 \le t \le T},</math> that, just as before, is a solution of

:<math>
dX_t \;=\; \mu(t, X_t)\,dt \;+\; \sigma(t, X_t)\,dW_t,
\quad
0 \le t \le T,
</math>

then if the [[expectation value]] is finite

:<math>
\int_{0}^{T}\,
  \mathbb{E}\!\Bigl[
    \bigl(\sigma(t, X_t)\,\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}(t, X_t)\bigr)^2
  \Bigr]\,
dt
\;<\;\infty,
</math>

then the Feynman–Kac formula is obtained:

:<math>
F(t,x)
\;=\;
\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\;\Phi(X_T)\,\big|\;X_t = x\bigr].
</math>

'''Proof.''' Apply [[Itô calculus|Itô's formula]] to <math>F(s, X_s)</math> for <math>t \le s \le T</math>:

:<math>
F(T, X_T)
\;=\;
F(t, X_t)
\;+\;
\int_{t}^{T}\!\Bigl\{
  \frac{\partial F}{\partial s}(s, X_s)
  \;+\;
  \mu(s, X_s)\,\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}(s, X_s)
  \;+\;
  \tfrac12\,\sigma^2(s, X_s)\,\frac{\partial^2 F}{\partial x^2}(s, X_s)
\Bigr\}\,ds
\;+\;
\int_{t}^{T}\!\sigma(s, X_s)\,\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}(s, X_s)\,dW_s.
</math>

Because <math>F</math> solves the PDE, the first integral is zero.  Taking [[conditional expectation]] and using the [[martingale (probability theory)|martingale property]] of the Itô integral gives

:<math>
\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[F(T, X_T)\,\big|\;X_t=x\bigr]
\;=\;
F(t, x).
</math>

Substitute <math>F(T, X_T) = \Phi(X_T)</math> to conclude

:<math>
F(t,x)
\;=\;
\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\;\Phi(X_T)\,\big|\;X_t = x\bigr].
</math>

== Derivation of the backward Kolmogorov equation ==
The Feynman–Kac representation can be used to find the PDE solved by the transition densities of solutions to SDEs. Suppose

:<math>
dX_t \;=\;
\mu(t, X_t)\,dt
\;+\;
\sigma(t, X_t)\,dW_t.
</math>

For any set <math>B</math>, define

:<math>
p_B(t, x;\,T)
\;\triangleq\;
\mathbb{P}\!\bigl[X_T \in B \,\mid\, X_t = x\bigr]
\;=\;
\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\mathbf{1}_B(X_T)\,\big|\;X_t = x\bigr].
</math>

By Feynman–Kac (under integrability conditions), taking <math>\Phi=\mathbf{1}_B</math>, then

:<math>
\frac{\partial p_B}{\partial t}(t, x;\,T)
\;+\;
A\,p_B(t, x;\,T)
\;=\;0,
\quad
p_B(T, x;\,T)
\;=\;\mathbf{1}_B(x),
</math>

where

:<math>
A\,f(t, x)
\;=\;
\mu(t, x)\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(t, x)
\;+\;
\tfrac12\,\sigma^2(t, x)\,\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(t, x).
</math>

Assuming [[Lebesgue measure]] as the reference, write <math>|B|</math> for its measure.  The transition density <math>p(t, x;\,T, y)</math> is

:<math>
p(t, x;\,T, y)
\;\triangleq\;
\lim_{B \to y}\,\frac{1}{|B|}\,\mathbb{P}\!\bigl[X_T \in B\,\mid\,X_t = x\bigr].
</math>

Then

:<math>
\frac{\partial p}{\partial t}(t, x;\,T, y)
\;+\;
A\,p(t, x;\,T, y)
\;=\;0,
\quad
p(t, x;\,T, y)
\;\to\;
\delta_y(x)
\quad
\text{as } t\;\to\;T.
</math>

== Derivation of the forward Kolmogorov equation ==

The Kolmogorov forward equation is

:<math>
\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\,p\bigl(t, x;\,T, y\bigr)
\;=\;
A^{*}\!\bigl[p\bigl(t, x;\,T, y\bigr)\bigr],
\quad
\lim_{T \to t}\,p(t,x;\,T,y)
\;=\;
\delta_{y}(x).
</math>

For <math>T > r > t</math>, the [[Markov property]] implies

:<math>
p(t, x;\,T, y)
\;=\;
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
  p\bigl(t, x;\,r, z\bigr)\,
  p\bigl(r, z;\,T, y\bigr)
\,dz.
</math>

Differentiate both sides w.r.t. <math>r</math>:

:<math>
0
\;=\;
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\Bigl[
  \frac{\partial}{\partial r}\,p\bigl(t, x;\,r, z\bigr)\,\cdot\,p\bigl(r, z;\,T, y\bigr)
  \;+\;
  p\bigl(t, x;\,r, z\bigr)\,\cdot\,
  \frac{\partial}{\partial r}\,p\bigl(r, z;\,T, y\bigr)
\Bigr]\,dz.
</math>

From the backward Kolmogorov equation:

:<math>
\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\,p\bigl(r, z;\,T, y\bigr)
\;=\;
-\,A\,p\bigl(r, z;\,T, y\bigr).
</math>

Substitute into the integral:

:<math>
0
\;=\;
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\Bigl[
  \frac{\partial}{\partial r}\,p\bigl(t, x;\,r, z\bigr)\,\cdot\,p\bigl(r, z;\,T, y\bigr)
  \;-\;
  p\bigl(t, x;\,r, z\bigr)\,\cdot\,
  A\,p\bigl(r, z;\,T, y\bigr)
\Bigr]
\,dz.
</math>

By definition of the [[adjoint operator]] <math>A^{*}</math>:

:<math>
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\bigl[
  \frac{\partial}{\partial r}\,p\bigl(t, x;\,r, z\bigr)
  \;-\;
  A^{*}\,p\bigl(t, x;\,r, z\bigr)
\bigr]\,
p\bigl(r, z;\,T, y\bigr)
\,dz
\;=\;
0.
</math>

Since <math>p(r,z;\,T,y)</math> can be arbitrary, the bracket must vanish:

:<math>
\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\,p\bigl(t, x;\,r,z\bigr)
\;=\;
A^{*}\bigl[p\bigl(t, x;\,r,z\bigr)\bigr].
</math>

Relabel <math>r \to T</math> and <math>z \to y</math>, yielding the forward Kolmogorov equation:

:<math>
\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\,p\bigl(t, x;\,T, y\bigr)
\;=\;
A^{*}\!\bigl[p\bigl(t, x;\,T, y\bigr)\bigr],
\quad
\lim_{T \to t}\,p(t,x;\,T,y)
\;=\;
\delta_{y}(x).
</math>

Finally,

:<math>
A^{*}\,g(x)
\;=\;
-\sum_{i}\,\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}
  \bigl[\mu_{i}(x)\,g(x)\bigr]
\;+\;
\frac12\,
\sum_{i,j}\,
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_{i}\,\partial x_{j}}
  \Bigl[
    \bigl(\sigma(x)\,\sigma(x)^{\mathsf{T}}\bigr)_{ij}\,g(x)
  \Bigr].
</math>
